sections.heading: Fracture mechanics, healing and the growing skeleton
sections.html:
Trauma questions on Step 1 test what breaks, what heals and what is damaged nearby. This section covers how bone fails and heals, why children's skeletons break differently, the fracture patterns that suggest abuse, and the physiology of compartment syndrome, fat embolism and blast injury.

How bone fails

  • Transverse fractures come from bending, oblique from compression with bending, and spiral from twisting.
  • Comminuted (three or more fragments) and segmental fractures mean high energy and more soft-tissue damage.
  • Avulsion fractures happen where a tendon or ligament pulls off its bony attachment, for example the base of the fifth metatarsal (peroneus brevis), the tibial spine (ACL) or the pelvic apophyses in adolescent sprinters.
  • Stress (fatigue) fractures come from repeated loading of normal bone: the metatarsals, tibia and femoral neck of runners and recruits. Low energy availability and amenorrhea raise the risk (the triad of disordered eating, menstrual dysfunction and low bone density in athletes).
  • Insufficiency fractures are normal loads on weak bone (osteoporosis), such as sacral or pubic ramus fractures in older adults. Pathologic fractures occur through a lesion such as a metastasis, myeloma or a cyst.
[[figure:s23f-fig070401-2]]

Fracture healing

  1. Hematoma and inflammation (days): bleeding from torn vessels forms a clot. Platelets and macrophages release PDGF, TGF-β and BMPs, and dead bone at the edges is resorbed.
  2. Soft callus (about 1–3 weeks): mesenchymal cells from the periosteum and marrow form fibrocartilage and hyaline cartilage, with new capillaries, that splints the gap.
  3. Hard callus: the cartilage is replaced by woven bone through endochondral ossification. Beneath the periosteum, bone forms directly (intramembranous).
  4. Remodeling over months to years: woven bone is replaced by lamellar bone along lines of stress.

With rigid fixation and compression, healing is "primary": osteons cross the fracture directly and little callus forms. Healing is delayed or fails with poor blood supply (scaphoid proximal pole, femoral neck, distal tibia), too much motion, infection, smoking, diabetes, malnutrition, vitamin D deficiency and possibly long-term high-dose NSAIDs or glucocorticoids.

The growing skeleton

Children's bones are more porous and bend more before they break. Their periosteum is thick and strong and makes callus quickly, so remodeling is fast. Typical patterns:

  • Torus (buckle): compression of the cortex, often the distal radial metaphysis; stable.
  • Greenstick: the tension side breaks and the compression side bends.
  • Plastic deformation: bowing without a visible fracture line (forearm).
  • Physeal (growth plate) fractures, described by the Salter–Harris system. The physis is weakest at the zone of hypertrophic chondrocytes, so most fractures run through it. Germinal (resting) cells lie on the epiphyseal side; injuries that cross them (types III and IV) or crush them (type V) risk growth arrest, a limb-length difference and angular deformity.
[[figure:s23f-fig070401-1]]
Salter–Harris typeFracture lineGrowth risk
IThrough the physis only (may look normal on x-ray)Low
II (commonest)Physis plus a metaphyseal fragmentLow
IIIPhysis plus the epiphysis, into the jointHigher; needs anatomic reduction
IVAcross metaphysis, physis and epiphysisHigh
VCrush of the physisHighest; often diagnosed late

Fracture patterns that suggest abuse

Some injuries need forces that ordinary infant care and household falls do not produce. The most specific are classic metaphyseal lesions ("corner" or "bucket-handle" fractures from shearing forces when an infant is shaken or a limb is pulled and twisted) and posterior rib fractures (the ribs are levered over the transverse processes when the chest is squeezed). Others are scapular, sternal and spinous process fractures, multiple fractures at different stages of healing, and any fracture in an infant who is not yet walking. Abuse is a pattern problem: interpret the history against the child's developmental stage.

Compartment syndrome physiology

Fascia does not stretch. Bleeding or edema inside a closed compartment raises the pressure until it exceeds the pressure in the thin-walled veins and capillaries. Venous outflow collapses, the arteriovenous gradient that drives perfusion disappears, and muscle and nerve become ischemic, even though a large artery passing through still carries a pulse. Ischemia increases capillary leak, so edema and pressure keep rising. Nerves fail first (paresthesias); muscle necrosis starts within a few hours and leads to rhabdomyolysis and, in the forearm, to fibrotic Volkmann ischemic contracture. Perfusion depends on the gap between diastolic pressure and compartment pressure, which is why hypotension makes compartment syndrome worse.

Fat embolism

Marrow fat enters torn venules after fractures of long bones or the pelvis, or during intramedullary reaming. In the lungs, globules block capillaries and lipase releases toxic free fatty acids that injure the endothelium (an ARDS-like picture). Globules that cross a patent foramen ovale or pass through the pulmonary capillaries reach the brain and skin. Fat stains with oil red O or Sudan black in frozen tissue.

Blast injury mechanisms

  • Primary: the overpressure wave damages gas-filled organs at air–tissue interfaces. It causes tympanic membrane rupture (commonest), blast lung (alveolar hemorrhage, pneumothorax, air embolism) and bowel contusion or perforation.
  • Secondary: flying fragments cause penetrating wounds.
  • Tertiary: the person is thrown against objects, causing blunt trauma, fractures and traumatic amputation.
  • Quaternary: everything else: burns, crush, toxic inhalation and worsening of chronic disease.

A palpable pulse does not exclude compartment syndrome. Compartment pressure blocks capillary and venous flow long before it can occlude an artery.

Salter–Harris type I fractures can have normal x-rays. Tenderness over a growth plate after injury in a child is treated as a type I fracture.

sections.heading: Anatomy of common injuries: shoulder, upper limb, knee, hip and spine
sections.html:
Injuries of the shoulder, elbow, hip, knee and spine are tested by asking which nerve, vessel or ligament is at risk. Learn the anatomy behind each classic injury.

Upper limb: fracture or dislocation and the structure at risk

InjuryStructure at riskDeficit
Anterior shoulder dislocation; surgical neck of humerus fractureAxillary nerve (C5–C6), posterior circumflex humeral arteryWeak abduction beyond about 15° (deltoid) and external rotation (teres minor); numb lateral shoulder
Midshaft or distal-third humerus fractureRadial nerve in the spiral groove, deep brachial arteryWrist and finger drop; numb dorsal first web space; triceps spared
Supracondylar humerus fracture (child)Anterior interosseous branch of the median nerve, brachial arteryCannot flex the thumb IP and index DIP joints (no "OK" sign); pulseless hand; risk of Volkmann contracture
Medial epicondyle fractureUlnar nerveWeak interossei, clawing of ring and little fingers, numb little finger
Hook of hamate fractureUlnar nerve in Guyon canalHand weakness without forearm involvement
Lunate dislocationMedian nerve in the carpal tunnelAcute carpal tunnel syndrome
Scaphoid waist fractureRetrograde blood supply from the dorsal branch of the radial arteryNonunion and osteonecrosis of the proximal pole

Shoulder and the rotator cuff

The four cuff muscles hold the humeral head in the shallow glenoid:

  • Supraspinatus: starts abduction (0–15°); suprascapular nerve; the tendon most often torn.
  • Infraspinatus: external rotation; suprascapular nerve.
  • Teres minor: external rotation; axillary nerve.
  • Subscapularis: internal rotation; upper and lower subscapular nerves.

The supraspinatus tendon runs beneath the coracoacromial arch. A hooked acromion, acromioclavicular osteophytes and aging tendon make it prone to impingement, degenerative tendinopathy and tears, mostly after age 40. A painful arc (about 60–120°) suggests subacromial impingement. Anterior dislocation (the commonest type) tears the anteroinferior labrum (a Bankart lesion) and dents the posterolateral humeral head on the glenoid rim (a Hill–Sachs lesion). Posterior dislocations follow seizures and electric shocks, because the strong internal rotators contract.

Knee

[[figure:s23f-fig070401-3]]
  • ACL (lateral femoral condyle to the anterior tibia) stops anterior tibial translation. It tears in noncontact pivoting and landing, with a pop and a hemarthrosis within hours. The Lachman test is the most sensitive exam.
  • PCL (medial femoral condyle to the posterior tibia) stops posterior translation. It is injured when the shin hits a dashboard or in a fall onto a flexed knee. Look for a posterior drawer and posterior sag.
  • MCL resists valgus stress (a blow to the lateral knee). It is attached to the medial meniscus, so the two are often injured together. LCL resists varus stress, and the common fibular nerve is nearby.
  • Menisci are fibrocartilage C-shapes that spread load. Their inner two-thirds have no blood supply and heal poorly. Tears cause joint-line pain, catching or locking, and a delayed effusion.

Hip and pelvis

  • Posterior hip dislocation (90% of dislocations; knee hits the dashboard) leaves the leg shortened, flexed, adducted and internally rotated. The sciatic nerve (usually its fibular division) is at risk, and the femoral head can lose its blood supply.
  • Femoral neck fractures (intracapsular) threaten the retinacular branches of the medial circumflex femoral artery. Intertrochanteric fractures are extracapsular, with good blood supply but more blood loss.
  • Gluteal injections in the upper outer quadrant avoid the sciatic nerve. Superior gluteal nerve injury weakens gluteus medius and minimus and causes a Trendelenburg gait.

Spine

  • In adults the spinal cord ends at about L1–L2; below that the canal holds the nerve roots of the cauda equina.
  • Cauda equina syndrome (a lower motor neuron lesion) causes saddle anesthesia, urinary retention with overflow, lost anal tone, and often asymmetric radicular leg weakness with reduced reflexes. Conus medullaris lesions start more suddenly and more symmetrically, with early sphincter loss and mixed upper and lower motor neuron signs.
  • Lumbar disc herniations are usually posterolateral, because the posterior longitudinal ligament is weakest there. They compress the root that exits one level below (an L4–L5 disc compresses L5). Far-lateral herniations hit the exiting root of the same level.
RootMotorReflexSensation
L4Knee extension, ankle inversionPatellarMedial leg
L5Great toe extension, ankle dorsiflexion, hip abductionNone reliableDorsum of foot, first web space
S1Plantar flexion, ankle eversionAchillesLateral foot, sole

Scoliosis is a lateral curve with vertebral rotation. Most cases in adolescents are idiopathic and polygenic, most often a right thoracic curve in girls. Rotation pushes the ribs backward on the convex side, which produces the rib hump seen on the forward-bend test. Neuromuscular curves (cerebral palsy, spinal muscular atrophy, Duchenne dystrophy) are long C-shaped curves that worsen after growth stops and can restrict lung function. Kyphosis is excessive forward curvature. Scheuermann kyphosis is a rigid adolescent kyphosis with wedged vertebrae from abnormal endplate growth. In older adults hyperkyphosis comes from osteoporotic wedge fractures.

Naadi memory aid for nerve risk around the humerus, from the top down: "Axillary at the neck, Radial in the groove, Median at the supracondyles, Ulnar at the medial epicondyle" (A-R-M-U).

In a posterolateral L4–L5 herniation, the patellar and Achilles reflexes may both be normal. The clue is weak great-toe extension and numbness over the dorsum of the foot.

sections.heading: Fractures, dislocations and orthopedic emergencies; hip fracture, falls, amputation and blast injury
sections.html:
Orthopedic emergencies, fracture care in older adults and amputation are tested on Step 2 CK as decisions: what to image, what to give, how fast to operate, and how to prevent the next injury.

First assessment of any injured limb

  • Follow ATLS priorities first. Pelvic and femoral fractures can bleed enough to cause shock: bind an unstable pelvis.
  • Examine and record skin integrity, pulses, capillary refill, motor and sensory function in every named nerve distribution, and compartment tension, before and after any reduction or splint.
  • Image the joint above and below the injury, with two orthogonal views.
  • Splint in the position found unless the limb is pulseless; then gently realign first.

Orthopedic emergencies

EmergencyRecognitionAction
Open fractureAny wound that communicates with the fractureIV antibiotics as soon as possible (a first-generation cephalosporin; broader gram-negative cover for heavily contaminated or high-grade wounds), tetanus prophylaxis, sterile dressing, splint, surgical irrigation and debridement
Acute compartment syndromePain out of proportion, pain on passive stretch, tense compartment; paresthesias; pulses often presentRemove casts and dressings, keep the limb at heart level, emergency fasciotomy (measure pressure if the exam is unreliable)
Vascular injuryAbsent pulse, expanding hematoma, low ankle-brachial indexReduce the fracture, then vascular imaging and repair
Hip dislocationShortened, rotated leg after high-energy injuryReduce urgently (within about 6 hours) to lower the risk of osteonecrosis; check sciatic nerve function
Cauda equina syndromeSaddle anesthesia, retention, bilateral sciaticaEmergency MRI and surgical decompression
Septic jointHot, swollen joint with feverAspirate, start antibiotics, surgical washout

Fat embolism syndrome appears 24–72 hours after long-bone or pelvic fractures. It causes hypoxemia, confusion and a petechial rash on the upper trunk, axillae and conjunctivae. Diagnosis is clinical. Treatment is supportive (oxygen, ventilation if needed). Early stabilization of femoral fractures lowers the risk.

Common fractures and dislocations

  • Scaphoid: a fall on an outstretched hand, then anatomic snuffbox tenderness. If initial x-rays are normal, put the wrist in a thumb spica splint and get MRI (or repeat films in 10–14 days). Displaced or proximal fractures need fixation.
  • Distal radius in older adults (dorsally displaced): closed reduction and casting, or fixation for unstable patterns. It is a sentinel fragility fracture, so start osteoporosis evaluation.
  • Fifth metacarpal neck ("boxer's") fracture: check for rotational deformity and for a fight bite over the knuckle (human bite: irrigate and give amoxicillin–clavulanate).
  • Anterior shoulder dislocation: get x-rays before and after closed reduction, and document axillary nerve function. Young athletes have a high recurrence rate and may need surgery. In older adults, test for an associated rotator cuff tear.
  • Posterior shoulder dislocation after a seizure or electric shock is easily missed on a single AP view. Get an axillary or scapular Y view.
  • Tibial shaft: watch for compartment syndrome for at least 24 hours.
  • Vertebral compression fracture in an older adult: analgesia, early mobilization and osteoporosis treatment. Calcitonin can reduce acute pain. Be alert for cord signs or red flags for malignancy.

Hip fracture in older adults

  • Presentation: a fall, groin pain, inability to bear weight, and a shortened, externally rotated leg (if displaced).
  • Imaging: if AP pelvis and lateral hip films are normal but suspicion stays high, MRI is the best test for an occult fracture (CT if MRI cannot be done).
  • Surgery within 24–48 hours lowers mortality, pain and complications. Only correct what is quickly reversible (anemia, volume, warfarin reversal if needed). Waiting for nonurgent tests causes harm.
    • Nondisplaced femoral neck: internal fixation.
    • Displaced femoral neck: hemiarthroplasty, or total hip arthroplasty in active, cognitively intact patients.
    • Intertrochanteric: sliding hip screw or cephalomedullary nail.
  • Peri-operative care: regional nerve block (fascia iliaca or femoral) to spare opioids, VTE prophylaxis, delirium prevention (orientation, sleep, avoiding benzodiazepines and anticholinergics, treating pain), pressure-injury prevention, early mobilization on day 1, and nutrition support.
  • Secondary prevention: start osteoporosis therapy (a bisphosphonate such as zoledronic acid once vitamin D is replete) without waiting for DXA, and assess falls risk.
  • Prognosis: about one in five older adults dies within a year, and many do not regain their previous mobility.

Falls in older adults

Ask every older adult about falls each year. For those who have fallen or are unsteady, check gait and balance (a timed up-and-go test), orthostatic vital signs, vision, feet and footwear, cognition and home hazards. Review medications that raise fall risk: sedative-hypnotics including "Z-drugs", benzodiazepines, antipsychotics, opioids, anticholinergics, tricyclics and excess antihypertensives or hypoglycemics. Exercise programs that train strength and balance prevent falls in community-dwelling older adults at higher risk.

Amputation and blast injury

  • Traumatic amputation: control bleeding with direct pressure, then a tourniquet. Wrap the part in saline-moistened gauze, seal it in a plastic bag and place the bag on ice (never directly on ice), and transfer to a replantation center.
  • Care after major limb amputation (most often from peripheral artery disease and diabetes):
    • Control edema with rigid dressings or shrinkers, check the residual limb skin every day, and manage pain.
    • Prevent contractures: hip and knee flexion contractures block prosthetic fitting. Do not put a pillow under the residual limb; lie prone regularly after a transfemoral amputation; keep the knee extended after a transtibial amputation.
    • Start rehabilitation early and give psychological support.
    • Treat phantom limb pain with gabapentinoids or tricyclics and mirror therapy. Phantom sensation is expected and harmless.
    • Look after the other limb in people with diabetes or vascular disease.
  • Blast casualties: triage by injury severity, not by visible wounds alone. A ruptured tympanic membrane shows exposure but its absence does not exclude blast lung. Look for blast lung (hypoxemia and infiltrates within hours; use cautious fluids, and watch for pneumothorax and air embolism with positive-pressure ventilation), delayed bowel perforation, crush and compartment syndromes, embedded fragments and traumatic brain injury. Give tetanus prophylaxis.

Delaying hip fracture surgery for nonurgent tests (echocardiography for a soft murmur in a stable patient, waiting for a direct oral anticoagulant to fully clear) causes more harm than it prevents. Operate within 24–48 hours.

Any older adult with a fall-related fracture needs three things before discharge: osteoporosis treatment, a falls-risk plan and a medication review.

furtherReading.statpearls: Falls and Fall Prevention in Older Adults

sections.heading: Pediatric orthopedics: physeal injury, nonaccidental trauma, the limping child and scoliosis
sections.html:
Pediatric orthopedics on Step 2 CK is about recognizing patterns by age: what an injured child's x-ray means, when a fracture suggests abuse, why a child limps, and when a spinal curve needs action.

Pediatric fractures

  • Torus (buckle) fractures of the distal radius are stable. A removable splint for about 3 weeks is enough, with no routine follow-up x-ray.
  • Greenstick fractures may need reduction if angulated.
  • Physeal injuries: Salter–Harris I and II are usually treated with closed reduction and casting. Types III and IV are intra-articular and need anatomic (often open) reduction. Follow all physeal injuries for growth disturbance.
  • Supracondylar humerus fracture (age 5–7 years, fall on an outstretched hand): check the radial pulse, hand perfusion and anterior interosseous nerve function. Displaced fractures need closed reduction and pinning. A pulseless, poorly perfused hand needs emergency reduction. Increasing forearm pain after treatment means compartment syndrome.
  • Radial head subluxation ("pulled elbow", age 1–4 years): the child holds the arm slightly flexed and pronated and will not use it after a pull on the hand. If the history is typical and there is no swelling or point tenderness, reduce it without x-ray by hyperpronation or supination with flexion.
  • Toddler's fracture: a nondisplaced spiral fracture of the distal tibia in a newly walking child after a minor twist. It is accidental when the history and development fit.
  • Clavicle fractures (including birth injury) heal well with a sling or no treatment.

Nonaccidental trauma (child physical abuse)

Red flags:

  • A history that is absent, changes, or does not fit the injury or the child's development ("rolled off the couch" in a 3-month-old who cannot roll).
  • A delay in seeking care.
  • Any fracture in a child who is not yet walking.
  • Classic metaphyseal lesions, posterior rib fractures, and multiple fractures of different ages.
  • Bruises in a child who is not cruising, or bruises on the torso, ears or neck, or patterned bruises.
  • Sentinel injuries such as frenulum tears in infants.

Workup:

  • A skeletal survey for all children under 2 years with suspected abuse, repeated in about 2 weeks to show healing fractures that were invisible at first.
  • Head imaging (CT or MRI) in infants, even without neurologic signs.
  • A dilated eye exam for retinal hemorrhages when head injury is suspected.
  • Abdominal trauma screening (liver enzymes, lipase, urinalysis).
  • Labs to exclude mimics: CBC and coagulation studies for bruising; calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, PTH and 25-hydroxyvitamin D for fractures.
  • Screen siblings and other children in the home.

Mimics include osteogenesis imperfecta (blue sclerae, wormian bones, family history), rickets and bleeding disorders. They are rarely the explanation. Report reasonable suspicion to child protective services (every clinician is a mandated reporter), keep the child safe, and document objectively. Hospital admission is appropriate when safety at home cannot be ensured.

The limping child

ConditionTypical ageKey featuresManagement
Septic arthritis of the hipAny, often under 3Fever, refuses to bear weight, high ESR/CRP and leukocytesEmergency aspiration, surgical drainage, IV antibiotics
Transient synovitis3–10After a viral illness, well-appearing, mild or no fever, can bear some weightNSAIDs and rest; recovers within days
Legg–Calvé–Perthes disease4–8, boysPainless or mildly painful limp, less abduction and internal rotation; flattened, sclerotic, fragmented femoral headObservation and range-of-motion therapy in young children; containment surgery for older children with extensive involvement
Slipped capital femoral epiphysis10–16, obese, around pubertyHip, thigh or knee pain; obligatory external rotation when the hip is flexedStop weight bearing; in situ screw fixation
Osgood–Schlatter diseaseAdolescent athletesTender tibial tubercleActivity modification; self-limited
Malignancy (leukemia, Ewing sarcoma)AnyNight pain, systemic symptoms, abnormal blood countCBC, imaging, referral

Knee pain in a child or adolescent can come from the hip (referred through the obturator nerve). Always examine the hip. In SCFE, an atypical age (under 10, or older than 16), a thin child or bilateral slips suggest an endocrine cause: hypothyroidism, growth hormone therapy or deficiency, or renal osteodystrophy. Unstable slips (the child cannot bear weight) carry a high risk of osteonecrosis. In Legg–Calvé–Perthes disease, onset before age 6 has a better outlook, and MRI shows changes before radiographs do.

Scoliosis and kyphosis

  • Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis is usually painless. The forward-bend test shows a rib or lumbar prominence. Measure it with a scoliometer (about 7° or more prompts imaging) and get a standing posteroanterior spine radiograph to measure the Cobb angle and skeletal maturity.
  • Management by Cobb angle and remaining growth: observe smaller curves with repeat radiographs. Brace curves of about 25–40° in skeletally immature patients to slow progression. Spinal fusion is considered for curves above about 45–50°.
  • Red flags that call for MRI: pain, a left thoracic curve, rapid progression, neurologic signs or abnormal reflexes, early onset (juvenile or infantile), or cutaneous signs over the spine. Look for syrinx, tethered cord or tumor.
  • Neuromuscular scoliosis in children with cerebral palsy, spinal muscular atrophy or muscular dystrophy affects sitting balance and breathing. Seating and bracing help, and fusion is often needed. Plan care with families and the disability team.
  • Postural kyphosis corrects when the patient stands up straight or lies prone. Scheuermann kyphosis is rigid, with wedging of consecutive vertebrae on lateral films. It is treated with exercise and bracing, and surgery for severe curves.

A "rolled off the bed" femur fracture in an infant who cannot roll is not an accident until proven otherwise: get a skeletal survey and report. Testing for osteogenesis imperfecta does not delay reporting.

Teens with knee pain and a limp need a hip exam and AP and frog-leg pelvic films. Missing SCFE is a classic error.

sections.heading: Back pain, sprains, strains, knee and shoulder injuries, and hospital-acquired contractures
sections.html:
Back pain, sprains, strains, contusions and shoulder and knee soft-tissue injuries are among the commonest reasons for primary-care and emergency visits. Step 2 CK rewards conservative care when it is appropriate and fast action on red flags.

Low back pain

  • Nonspecific (mechanical) low back pain: most acute episodes improve within weeks. If there are no red flags, do not image in the first 6 weeks. Treat with reassurance, staying active, heat, NSAIDs and short-term skeletal muscle relaxants if needed. Avoid bed rest and opioids. Physical therapy, spinal manipulation, yoga and exercise help subacute and chronic pain.
  • Lumbar radiculopathy (sciatica): a positive straight-leg raise, with dermatomal pain and deficits. Most cases improve over 6 weeks with conservative care. MRI is for progressive or severe deficits, or persistent pain when surgery or an epidural injection is being considered.
  • Lumbar spinal stenosis (older adults): neurogenic claudication, meaning buttock and leg pain on standing and walking that is relieved by sitting or bending forward (leaning on a shopping cart). Pedal pulses are normal. MRI confirms it; treatment is physical therapy, then decompression for disabling symptoms.
  • Spondylolysis and spondylolisthesis in adolescent athletes (gymnasts, football linemen): extension-related low back pain from a pars interarticularis stress fracture.
Red flagConcernNext step
Saddle anesthesia, urinary retention, fecal incontinence, bilateral or progressive leg weaknessCauda equina syndromeEmergency MRI and surgical decompression
History of cancer, weight loss, night pain, age over 50Metastasis, myelomaMRI; dexamethasone and urgent oncology input for cord compression
Fever, injection drug use, recent bacteremia, immunosuppression, dialysisEpidural abscess, vertebral osteomyelitisMRI with contrast, blood cultures, ESR/CRP, early surgery if there are deficits
Minor trauma with osteoporosis or long-term glucocorticoidsCompression fractureRadiographs
Morning stiffness, better with exercise, onset before 40Axial spondyloarthritisSacroiliac imaging, HLA-B27 (covered with inflammatory disease)

Sprains, strains and contusions

  • A sprain is a ligament injury, graded I (stretch), II (partial tear) or III (complete tear). A strain is an injury of the muscle–tendon unit, typically the hamstring, calf or quadriceps, at the musculotendinous junction during eccentric contraction.
  • Ankle inversion sprain: the anterior talofibular ligament is injured first, then the calcaneofibular. Use the Ottawa ankle and foot rules: x-ray if the patient cannot bear weight for four steps both immediately and when examined, or has bone tenderness at the posterior edge or tip of either malleolus, the navicular or the base of the fifth metatarsal. Functional treatment (a brace, early weight bearing and balance exercises) beats rigid immobilization. A "high ankle" (syndesmotic) sprain recovers more slowly. Squeezing the calf hurts at the ankle.
  • Muscle contusions: a large thigh hematoma can calcify (myositis ossificans). Avoid aggressive massage early. A severe contusion can also cause compartment syndrome.

Knee injuries

  • Acute hemarthrosis (swelling within hours) means an ACL tear, a fracture or patellar dislocation until proven otherwise. Use the Ottawa knee rules for x-ray. MRI defines ligament and meniscal damage. Young athletes who pivot usually choose ACL reconstruction; less active patients may do well with rehabilitation alone.
  • Meniscal tears: in younger patients, traumatic twisting tears with true locking need arthroscopic repair. In middle-aged and older adults, degenerative tears with osteoarthritis are treated with physical therapy, because arthroscopic partial meniscectomy adds little.
  • MCL sprains heal with a hinged brace and early motion. Patellar dislocation (adolescent girls, lateral displacement) is reduced by extending the knee.
  • Patellar or quadriceps tendon rupture causes inability to extend the knee straight. It needs early surgical repair. Risks include fluoroquinolones, glucocorticoids, CKD and diabetes.

Shoulder: rotator cuff disease

  • Tendinopathy and impingement (overhead workers, people over 40): lateral shoulder pain, a painful arc and pain at night. Strength is preserved apart from pain. Treat with physical therapy (cuff and scapular strengthening), NSAIDs and a subacromial glucocorticoid injection if needed.
  • Full-thickness tear: true weakness (positive drop-arm test, external rotation lag sign), sometimes after a fall in older adults. Image with MRI or ultrasound. Early surgical repair is offered for acute traumatic tears in active patients; chronic degenerative tears in older adults often do well with therapy.
  • Also consider adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder: loss of active and passive motion, linked to diabetes and thyroid disease), acromioclavicular injury, biceps rupture ("Popeye" deformity) and referred pain from the neck or diaphragm.

Hospital-acquired contractures

Immobility for days to weeks lets muscles and joint capsules shorten. The risk is highest after stroke, spinal cord or brain injury, burns and long ICU stays, and in older adults. Contractures impair hygiene, transfers, seating and walking, and promote pressure injuries. Prevention:

  • Position joints carefully (ankles at 90° to prevent equinus, hips and knees extended, shoulders abducted).
  • Range-of-motion exercises at least daily, early mobilization, and splints or orthoses.
  • Treat spasticity (stretching, oral baclofen or tizanidine, botulinum toxin for focal spasticity).
  • Control pain.

Heterotopic ossification (bone in soft tissue around the hip or elbow after brain or spinal cord injury, burns or hip arthroplasty) also limits motion. NSAIDs or radiation can prevent it in high-risk surgical patients.

Imaging uncomplicated acute low back pain does not improve outcomes and finds incidental disc bulges that lead to unnecessary procedures.

Weakness separates a cuff tear from tendinopathy. If pain limits testing, a subacromial lidocaine injection that removes the pain without restoring strength points to a tear.

sets.title: An older adult who cannot bear weight after a fall

items.stemHtml: A 12-year-old boy falls on his outstretched right hand while skateboarding. The distal right forearm is swollen and tender. A radiograph shows a fracture line that runs transversely through the distal radial growth plate and then exits proximally through the metaphysis, leaving a triangular metaphyseal fragment attached to the epiphysis. The articular surface is intact. Which of the following best classifies this injury? (See the Salter–Harris figure.)
items.explanationHtml:
A fracture through the physis that exits through the metaphysis, carrying a metaphyseal fragment with the epiphysis, is Salter–Harris type II, the commonest physeal fracture. The germinal layer stays with the epiphysis, so growth disturbance is uncommon, and closed reduction and casting usually suffice.

Takeaway: type II = physis plus metaphysis; types III and IV enter the joint and need anatomic reduction.

whyNot.A: Type I runs only through the physis without any bony fragment and may look normal on x-ray.
whyNot.C: Type III runs through the physis and then the epiphysis into the joint; this fracture spares the articular surface.
whyNot.D: Type IV crosses metaphysis, physis and epiphysis, entering the joint.
whyNot.E: Type V is a crush of the physis without a displaced fracture line and is often recognized only when growth arrest appears.

items.objective: Classify a physeal fracture with a metaphyseal fragment as Salter–Harris type II.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old man falls from a ladder onto his right arm. Radiographs show a spiral fracture of the distal third of the humeral shaft. Which of the following examination findings is most likely if a nerve was injured by this fracture?
options: Inability to extend the wrist and fingers
Clawing of the ring and little fingers
Weak elbow flexion with numbness of the lateral forearm
Weak thumb opposition with thenar numbness
items.explanationHtml:
The radial nerve runs in the spiral groove and then pierces the lateral intermuscular septum at the distal third of the humerus, where it is tethered and easily injured by shaft fractures. Injury below the branches to triceps causes wrist drop and finger drop, with numbness over the dorsal first web space; elbow extension is spared. Most of these palsies are neurapraxias that recover.

Takeaway: humeral shaft fracture: check radial nerve function (wrist and finger extension).

whyNot.B: Weak abduction beyond 15° reflects deltoid weakness from axillary nerve injury, typical of surgical neck fractures and anterior shoulder dislocation.
whyNot.C: Clawing of the ring and little fingers results from ulnar nerve injury, typical of medial epicondyle fractures.
whyNot.D: The musculocutaneous nerve runs in the anterior arm muscles and is rarely injured by shaft fractures.
whyNot.E: Median nerve injury with thenar weakness follows supracondylar fractures or wrist injuries, not shaft fractures.

items.objective: Link humeral shaft fractures to radial nerve injury and wrist drop.

items.stemHtml: A 27-year-old man has an anterior dislocation of the left shoulder while playing rugby. After reduction, he has numbness over a patch of skin on the lateral upper arm. Weakness of abduction is also suspected. Injury to the nerve responsible for these findings would most likely also weaken which of the following muscles?
items.explanationHtml:
Anterior dislocation stretches the axillary nerve as it passes below the humeral head through the quadrangular space. The axillary nerve supplies the deltoid (abduction beyond about 15°) and teres minor (external rotation), and its superior lateral brachial cutaneous branch supplies the skin over the lower deltoid.

Takeaway: the axillary nerve supplies deltoid and teres minor; test sensation over the lateral shoulder after dislocation.

whyNot.A: Supraspinatus is supplied by the suprascapular nerve, which is not stretched by anterior dislocation.
whyNot.B: Infraspinatus is also supplied by the suprascapular nerve.
whyNot.D: Subscapularis is supplied by the upper and lower subscapular nerves from the posterior cord.
whyNot.E: Latissimus dorsi is supplied by the thoracodorsal nerve.

items.objective: Identify the muscles supplied by the axillary nerve.

items.stemHtml: A 59-year-old house painter has had 3 months of right shoulder pain that wakes him at night and is worst when he reaches overhead. Pain occurs between about 60° and 120° of abduction. With his arms abducted to 90°, flexed forward 30° and internally rotated (thumbs down), he cannot resist downward pressure on the right. When the examiner lowers his arm from 90° of abduction, he cannot hold it, and it drops. Which tendon is most likely torn?
items.explanationHtml:
Painful arc, weakness on the empty-can (Jobe) test and a positive drop-arm test point to a tear of the supraspinatus tendon, the commonest rotator cuff tear. The tendon passes through the narrow subacromial space beneath the coracoacromial arch, where it is compressed with overhead work and degenerates with age.

Takeaway: a painful arc, a weak empty-can test and a drop-arm sign indicate a supraspinatus tear.

whyNot.B: Infraspinatus tears weaken external rotation with the arm at the side and cause an external rotation lag sign.
whyNot.C: Teres minor is rarely torn alone and mainly assists external rotation.
whyNot.D: Subscapularis tears weaken internal rotation and are detected by the lift-off or belly-press tests.
whyNot.E: Biceps long-head rupture causes a bulge in the arm ("Popeye" deformity) rather than weak abduction with a drop-arm sign.

items.objective: Localize a rotator cuff tear to the supraspinatus by examination.

items.stemHtml: A 31-year-old woman is a front-seat passenger in a car crash, and her flexed right knee strikes the dashboard. The right knee is swollen. With the hips flexed to 45° and the knees to 90°, the right tibia sags backward relative to the left, and it can be pushed further back with gentle force. Valgus and varus stress tests are normal. Which structure is most likely injured?
items.explanationHtml:
A blow to the front of the proximal tibia with the knee flexed drives the tibia backward and tears the posterior cruciate ligament, which runs from the medial femoral condyle to the posterior tibia and prevents posterior translation. Posterior sag and a positive posterior drawer test confirm it.

Takeaway: dashboard injury with posterior sag = PCL tear.

whyNot.A: ACL tears allow anterior translation (positive Lachman and anterior drawer) and usually follow noncontact pivoting.
whyNot.C: MCL injury causes laxity to valgus stress, which is normal here.
whyNot.D: LCL injury causes laxity to varus stress, which is normal here.
whyNot.E: Patellar tendon rupture prevents active knee extension and leaves a high-riding patella; it does not cause posterior tibial translation.

items.objective: Recognize posterior cruciate ligament injury from mechanism and examination.

items.stemHtml: A 25-year-old man has a closed tibial shaft fracture from a motorcycle crash. Eight hours later he has escalating leg pain and pain with passive toe flexion. The dorsalis pedis pulse is strong, and capillary refill is normal. Blood pressure is 96/50 mm Hg after blood loss. Which of the following best explains how muscle ischemia develops in this condition despite the palpable pulse?
options: Thrombosis of the anterior tibial artery at the fracture site
Compartment pressure exceeding venous and capillary pressure, collapsing local perfusion
Embolization of marrow fat into the muscle arterioles
Reflex arterial vasospasm triggered by pain fibers
Direct laceration of muscle by bone fragments
items.explanationHtml:
Bleeding and edema inside the unyielding fascial compartment raise pressure until thin-walled veins and capillaries collapse. Outflow stops, the arteriovenous gradient that drives capillary perfusion is lost, and nerves and muscle become ischemic even though the main artery, whose pressure is much higher, keeps a palpable pulse. Low blood pressure narrows the gap between diastolic and compartment pressure, so hypotension speeds ischemia.

Takeaway: compartment syndrome is a microcirculatory failure; pulses persist until very late.

whyNot.A: Arterial thrombosis causes a pale, cold, pulseless foot; this foot has a strong pulse and normal capillary refill.
whyNot.C: Fat embolism affects the lungs, brain and skin rather than causing a tense, painful compartment.
whyNot.D: Vasospasm does not explain a tense compartment with pain on passive stretch, and the pulse is strong.
whyNot.E: Direct muscle laceration is part of the initial injury but does not explain hours-later escalating pain and stretch pain.

items.objective: Explain the microcirculatory pathophysiology of acute compartment syndrome.

items.stemHtml: A 22-year-old man has a closed fracture of the left femoral shaft from a motorcycle crash and is placed in skeletal traction. Thirty-six hours later he becomes confused and short of breath. SpO2 is 84% on room air. There are petechiae over the axillae, upper chest and conjunctivae. Platelet count is 96,000/mm3. Chest radiograph shows diffuse bilateral opacities. CT pulmonary angiography shows no filling defects. Which of the following would most likely be found in his pulmonary capillaries?
options: Lipid globules that stain with oil red O
Laminated thrombus with lines of Zahn
Gas bubbles in the right ventricle
items.explanationHtml:
Hypoxemia, confusion and an upper-body petechial rash 24–72 hours after a long-bone fracture are fat embolism syndrome. Marrow fat enters torn veins and lodges in the pulmonary microcirculation; lipase releases free fatty acids that injure capillaries, and fat crossing into the systemic circulation causes cerebral and skin findings. Fat is shown in frozen sections with oil red O or Sudan stains.

Takeaway: fat embolism syndrome = respiratory failure, neurologic change and petechiae after long-bone fracture.

whyNot.B: Thromboembolism would usually be visible on CT angiography and does not cause petechiae.
whyNot.C: Fetal squames and mucin indicate amniotic fluid embolism during or after delivery.
whyNot.D: Air embolism follows central line or chest injury and appears suddenly, not after a 36-hour delay with petechiae.
whyNot.E: Septic emboli come from endocarditis or septic thrombophlebitis, with fever and nodular cavitating lesions.

items.objective: Recognize the pathology of fat embolism syndrome after long-bone fracture.

items.stemHtml: A 44-year-old warehouse worker has 2 weeks of low back pain radiating down the back of the right thigh and lateral calf to the top of the foot. MRI shows a posterolateral disc herniation at L4–L5 compressing a nerve root in the lateral recess. Which of the following findings is most likely on examination?
options: Weak extension of the right great toe
items.explanationHtml:
Posterolateral lumbar herniations compress the traversing root that exits one level below, so an L4–L5 herniation affects L5. L5 supplies extensor hallucis longus (great toe extension), ankle dorsiflexion and hip abduction, and sensation over the dorsum of the foot and first web space. No major reflex depends on L5.

Takeaway: L4–L5 posterolateral disc = L5 root: weak great-toe extension, numb dorsum of the foot, reflexes preserved.

whyNot.A: The Achilles reflex depends on S1, typically affected by an L5–S1 herniation.
whyNot.B: The patellar reflex depends on L4, typically affected by an L3–L4 herniation.
whyNot.D: Hip flexion depends mainly on L1–L3 roots, which are not compressed at L4–L5.
whyNot.E: Perianal numbness indicates sacral root compression in cauda equina syndrome, which would be an emergency with bilateral or sphincter signs.

items.objective: Localize an L4–L5 posterolateral disc herniation to the L5 root.

items.stemHtml: A 29-year-old woman was 6 meters from an explosion in an enclosed train carriage. She has no penetrating wounds. Two hours later she has dyspnea, chest pain and hemoptysis. SpO2 is 88% on room air. Both tympanic membranes are perforated. Chest radiograph shows bilateral central perihilar opacities. Which of the following mechanisms best explains her lung injury?
options: A pressure wave damaging tissue at air–tissue interfaces
Blunt impact after being thrown against a wall
Aspiration of gastric contents during loss of consciousness
items.explanationHtml:
Primary blast injury comes from the overpressure wave, which damages gas-filled organs where tissues of different density meet: the middle ear, the lungs (alveolar hemorrhage, pulmonary contusion, pneumothorax, air embolism) and the bowel. Enclosed spaces amplify the wave. Blast lung typically appears within hours as hypoxemia with central perihilar ("butterfly") opacities.

Takeaway: primary blast injury hits air-filled organs: ears, lungs and bowel.

whyNot.B: Fragment injury (secondary blast) produces penetrating wounds, which she does not have.
whyNot.C: Being thrown (tertiary blast) causes blunt trauma and fractures; it can bruise the lung but does not explain bilateral ear injury with central opacities in an unbruised patient.
whyNot.D: Toxic inhalation (quaternary) causes airway burns, carbon monoxide or cyanide poisoning, with soot and airway symptoms rather than hemoptysis from alveolar rupture.
whyNot.E: Aspiration requires reduced consciousness and causes dependent opacities, not this picture.

items.objective: Classify blast injury mechanisms and recognize primary blast lung.

items.stemHtml: An 81-year-old woman tripped over her cat at home 4 hours ago and now has right groin pain. She cannot bear weight on the right leg. She lives independently and takes amlodipine. The right leg is not shortened or rotated, but passive internal rotation of the hip causes severe groin pain. Anteroposterior pelvis and lateral right hip radiographs show diffuse osteopenia and no fracture line. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: Discharge with analgesia and a walker
items.explanationHtml:
An older adult who cannot bear weight with groin pain after a fall has a hip fracture until proven otherwise, even when radiographs are normal; a meaningful share of hip fractures are occult on initial films. MRI is the most sensitive and specific test and can be done promptly so that surgery is not delayed. CT is the alternative when MRI is not possible.

Takeaway: normal x-rays with high suspicion of hip fracture: MRI the same day.

whyNot.B: Discharging a patient who cannot bear weight risks displacement of an occult fracture, which then needs arthroplasty instead of fixation.
whyNot.C: Waiting 2 weeks leaves her immobile and at risk of displacement, delirium and thromboembolism.
whyNot.D: A bone scan may be falsely negative for several days in older adults and is less specific than MRI.
whyNot.E: Ultrasound can show an effusion but cannot reliably diagnose or exclude a fracture.

items.objective: Use MRI to find an occult hip fracture when radiographs are normal.

items.stemHtml: MRI in the patient from the previous item shows a nondisplaced fracture of the right femoral neck. She is alert and oriented. Hemoglobin is 12.1 g/dL, creatinine 0.9 mg/dL and ECG shows sinus rhythm. She has a soft systolic murmur that is unchanged from records 2 years ago and no cardiac symptoms. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
options: Skin traction and bed rest for 6 weeks
Echocardiography and cardiology review before any surgery
Physical therapy with weight bearing as tolerated
items.explanationHtml:
Nondisplaced femoral neck fractures in older adults are treated with internal fixation (cannulated screws or a sliding hip screw), which preserves the femoral head and allows early mobilization. Surgery within 24–48 hours lowers mortality and complications. A stable, unchanged murmur without symptoms does not justify delay.

Takeaway: hip fractures in older adults are surgical emergencies of the 24–48-hour kind; fix nondisplaced femoral neck fractures, replace displaced ones.

whyNot.B: Older adults cannot reliably stay non-weight-bearing, and nonoperative care has high rates of displacement and complications.
whyNot.C: Prolonged bed rest causes pneumonia, pressure injuries, VTE, delirium and loss of function, and has no role in modern hip fracture care.
whyNot.D: Preoperative echocardiography for an asymptomatic, unchanged murmur delays surgery without improving outcomes.
whyNot.E: Unprotected weight bearing on an unfixed femoral neck fracture risks displacement and osteonecrosis.

items.objective: Fix a nondisplaced femoral neck fracture surgically within 24–48 hours.

items.stemHtml: The patient from the previous items has screw fixation of her femoral neck fracture and is walking with a frame on postoperative day 4. She has never had a DXA scan or osteoporosis treatment. Serum calcium is 9.2 mg/dL, creatinine 0.8 mg/dL and 25-hydroxyvitamin D is in the sufficient range. Which of the following is the most appropriate step to reduce her risk of another fracture?
options: Obtain DXA in 12 months and treat if the T-score is −2.5 or lower
items.explanationHtml:
A low-trauma hip fracture establishes osteoporosis regardless of bone density, and the risk of a second fracture is highest in the following 1–2 years. Treatment should start without waiting for DXA. A bisphosphonate (often IV zoledronic acid after the immediate postoperative period, or oral alendronate) is first line once calcium and vitamin D are adequate, together with a falls-prevention plan.

Takeaway: after a fragility hip fracture, start osteoporosis treatment before discharge or soon after; do not wait for DXA.

whyNot.B: Waiting a year leaves her untreated during the period of highest risk, and her fracture already defines osteoporosis.
whyNot.C: Calcium alone does not meaningfully reduce fracture risk in established osteoporosis.
whyNot.D: Raloxifene reduces vertebral but not hip fractures and increases VTE risk after surgery.
whyNot.E: Calcitonin has weak antifracture efficacy and is not recommended for fracture prevention.

items.objective: Start osteoporosis treatment promptly after a fragility hip fracture.

items.stemHtml: A 3-month-old girl is brought to the emergency department because she has been crying and not moving her left leg since the previous evening. Her father says she rolled off the sofa onto a carpeted floor. She was born at term, and her development is normal for age; she cannot yet roll over. She has a small bruise on the right cheek. The left thigh is swollen. A radiograph shows a spiral fracture of the left femoral shaft. Sclerae are white. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in addition to treating the fracture?
options: Skeletal survey and a report to child protective services
Genetic testing for osteogenesis imperfecta before any report
Discharge home with a Pavlik harness and follow-up in 1 week
Bone density scan of the lumbar spine
items.explanationHtml:
A femur fracture in a 3-month-old who cannot roll, with a mechanism that does not fit her development and a facial bruise in a non-mobile infant, is highly concerning for physical abuse. The next steps are a complete skeletal survey (repeated in about 2 weeks), head imaging and an eye exam in infants this age, screening labs for mimics, and a report of reasonable suspicion to child protective services. Clinicians are mandated reporters; certainty is not required.

Takeaway: any fracture in a non-ambulatory infant with an implausible history: skeletal survey and report.

whyNot.B: Osteogenesis imperfecta is a rare mimic; tests can be sent, but they must not delay reporting or protecting the child.
whyNot.C: A Pavlik harness treats some infant femur fractures, but sending her home without addressing safety could expose her to further injury.
whyNot.D: Bone density testing is not a standard step in evaluating suspected abuse in infants.
whyNot.E: The femur fracture is already diagnosed; the priority is finding other occult injuries throughout the skeleton.

items.objective: Evaluate and report suspected child physical abuse in an infant with a femur fracture.

items.stemHtml: A 45-year-old man has had worsening low back pain for 3 days after moving furniture. Since this morning he has pain down both legs, numbness "where he sits" and has not passed urine for 10 hours. Examination shows reduced sensation over the perineum and buttocks, weak ankle plantar flexion bilaterally, absent Achilles reflexes and reduced anal sphincter tone. Bladder scan shows 900 mL of urine. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step after bladder catheterization?
options: Emergency MRI of the lumbosacral spine
NSAIDs, activity as tolerated and review in 2 weeks
Plain radiographs of the lumbar spine
items.explanationHtml:
Saddle anesthesia, urinary retention, bilateral radicular weakness, lost ankle reflexes and reduced anal tone are cauda equina syndrome, most often from a large central disc herniation. Emergency MRI confirms the level and cause, and surgical decompression should follow as soon as possible, because outcome for bladder function depends on early decompression.

Takeaway: red-flag back pain with saddle anesthesia and retention needs emergency MRI and decompression.

whyNot.B: Conservative care is for uncomplicated back pain; delay risks permanent bladder, bowel and sexual dysfunction.
whyNot.C: Radiographs do not show discs or nerve roots and would delay the definitive test.
whyNot.D: EMG is not an emergency test and does not show compression.
whyNot.E: Epidural injections treat radicular pain, not compressive cauda equina syndrome.

items.objective: Order emergency MRI for suspected cauda equina syndrome.

items.stemHtml:
A 79-year-old woman is seen after her second fall in 4 months; she tripped on the way to the bathroom at night. She has no injury today. She has hypertension, type 2 diabetes, hyperlipidemia and insomnia. Her medications are shown.

MedicationDose
Lisinopril10 mg daily
Metformin500 mg twice daily
Atorvastatin20 mg daily
Zolpidem10 mg at bedtime
Omeprazole20 mg daily

Blood pressure is 134/78 mm Hg lying and 130/76 mm Hg standing. Hemoglobin A1c is 7.1%. Timed up-and-go is 15 seconds. Vision with glasses is 20/30 in both eyes. Which of the following changes in her medications is most likely to reduce her risk of falls?
items.explanationHtml:
Sedative-hypnotics, including "Z-drugs" such as zolpidem, impair balance, reaction time and alertness at night and are strongly associated with falls and hip fractures in older adults; they are on lists of drugs to avoid in this age group. A night-time fall on the way to the bathroom fits. Taper and stop it, and treat insomnia with cognitive behavioural therapy and sleep hygiene. She has no orthostatic hypotension, and her diabetes regimen carries little hypoglycemia risk. Add a strength and balance exercise program.

Takeaway: in older adults who fall, deprescribe sedative-hypnotics first.

whyNot.B: Lisinopril could contribute through orthostasis, but her standing blood pressure is stable, and it protects her kidneys in diabetes.
whyNot.C: Metformin alone rarely causes hypoglycemia, and her A1c is at a reasonable target.
whyNot.D: Statin myalgia can cause weakness, but she has no muscle symptoms, and statins do not meaningfully raise fall risk.
whyNot.E: Long-term PPIs have some bone-health concerns, but they do not affect balance or alertness.

items.objective: Identify and deprescribe sedative-hypnotics to prevent falls in older adults.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old warehouse worker has had low back pain for 5 days after lifting a heavy box. The pain is in the lower back and right buttock and worsens with bending. He has no leg numbness, weakness, bladder or bowel symptoms, fever, weight loss or history of cancer or injection drug use. Examination shows paraspinal tenderness and spasm, a negative straight-leg raise test and normal strength, sensation and reflexes. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
options: An NSAID and advice to stay active
items.explanationHtml:
Acute mechanical low back pain without red flags usually improves within a few weeks. The best care is reassurance, staying active (including work with modified duties), heat and an NSAID, with a short course of a muscle relaxant if spasm is severe. Imaging in the first 6 weeks does not improve outcomes.

Takeaway: no red flags, no imaging: NSAIDs, heat and staying active.

whyNot.B: MRI often shows incidental disc findings and is reserved for red flags or persistent radicular symptoms in surgical candidates.
whyNot.C: Bed rest slows recovery compared with staying active.
whyNot.D: Opioids have no better effect on function than NSAIDs and add risks of dependence and adverse effects.
whyNot.E: Radiographs are not useful without red flags such as trauma, osteoporosis or suspected cancer.

items.objective: Manage acute low back pain without red flags conservatively and without imaging.

items.stemHtml: A 48-year-old carpenter fell from a ladder 3 weeks ago, landing on his outstretched left arm. Since then he cannot lift his arm to reach shelves. Radiographs at the time showed no fracture or dislocation. Passive range of motion of the shoulder is full. Active abduction is weak, he cannot hold the arm at 90° of abduction when it is released, and external rotation with the arm at his side is weak with a lag. Sensation over the lateral shoulder is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: Physical therapy for 3 months, then reassessment
items.explanationHtml:
Sudden weakness of abduction and external rotation after a fall, with full passive motion, a positive drop-arm test and an external rotation lag, indicates an acute full-thickness rotator cuff tear involving the supraspinatus and infraspinatus. In a younger, active patient, prompt imaging (MRI or ultrasound) and early surgical referral are recommended, because acute traumatic tears do best with early repair before the tendon retracts and the muscle atrophies.

Takeaway: acute traumatic cuff tear with weakness in an active patient: image promptly and refer for repair.

whyNot.B: Therapy first suits degenerative tears or tendinopathy in older patients; delaying an acute traumatic tear risks retraction and poorer repair.
whyNot.C: A glucocorticoid injection may relieve impingement pain but does not restore a torn tendon and can weaken tendon tissue.
whyNot.D: Prolonged immobilization causes stiffness and does not heal a full-thickness tear.
whyNot.E: Normal sensation and a typical traumatic history point to the shoulder rather than a cervical radiculopathy.

items.objective: Image and refer early for an acute traumatic full-thickness rotator cuff tear.

items.stemHtml: A 19-year-old college basketball player rolled his right ankle inward landing from a jump 2 hours ago. He walked off the court unassisted and can take four steps in the emergency department with a limp. There is swelling and tenderness anterior and inferior to the lateral malleolus. There is no tenderness at the posterior edge or tip of either malleolus, the navicular or the base of the fifth metatarsal. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
options: Ankle brace and early weight bearing
MRI of the ankle within 1 week
items.explanationHtml:
An inversion sprain of the anterior talofibular ligament with no bony tenderness at the Ottawa sites and the ability to bear weight for four steps does not need radiographs. Functional treatment (a lace-up or stirrup brace, ice and elevation for the first days, early weight bearing and balance and strengthening exercises) gives faster return to activity than immobilization.

Takeaway: use the Ottawa rules to skip unnecessary x-rays; treat ankle sprains functionally.

whyNot.B: He meets none of the Ottawa criteria, so radiographs would almost certainly be normal.
whyNot.C: Rigid casting of a lateral ankle sprain delays recovery compared with functional treatment.
whyNot.D: MRI is for persistent symptoms or suspected osteochondral or syndesmotic injury, not an acute uncomplicated sprain.
whyNot.E: Surgical repair is rarely needed and is reserved for chronic instability after rehabilitation fails.

items.objective: Apply the Ottawa ankle rules and functional treatment for a lateral ankle sprain.

items.stemHtml: A 6-year-old boy has had an intermittent limp for 2 months. He complains of mild pain in the right thigh and knee after playing. He has had no fever or recent illness. He is thin and active. Abduction and internal rotation of the right hip are limited; the knee is normal. Temperature is 36.8°C (98.2°F). CBC and ESR are normal. Anteroposterior and frog-leg lateral pelvic radiographs show a smaller, flattened and dense right femoral head with a subchondral lucent line. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
A painless or mildly painful limp in a 4–8-year-old boy, with limited abduction and internal rotation, normal inflammatory markers and a flattened, sclerotic femoral head with a subchondral fracture line, is Legg–Calvé–Perthes disease: idiopathic osteonecrosis of the capital femoral epiphysis. Management aims to keep the femoral head round and contained in the acetabulum: activity modification and range-of-motion therapy, with containment surgery for older children or extensive disease.

Takeaway: limp in a young boy with a flattened, dense femoral head = Perthes disease; thigh or knee pain can come from the hip.

whyNot.B: SCFE occurs in obese adolescents around puberty and shows displacement of the epiphysis on the metaphysis, not flattening of the head.
whyNot.C: Transient synovitis is short-lived (days), follows a viral illness and shows no bony changes.
whyNot.D: Septic arthritis causes fever, refusal to bear weight and raised inflammatory markers.
whyNot.E: Developmental dysplasia presents in infancy with hip instability or later with a shallow acetabulum, not a dense, flattened femoral head.

items.objective: Recognize Legg–Calvé–Perthes disease by age, examination and radiographs.

items.stemHtml: A 12-year-old girl is seen for a sports physical. She has no back pain and has not yet started menstruating. On the forward-bend test, the right side of her upper back is more prominent; a scoliometer reading is 9°. Her shoulders and waist creases are mildly asymmetric. Neurologic examination, including abdominal reflexes, is normal, and there are no skin lesions over the spine. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: Standing posteroanterior radiograph of the whole spine
items.explanationHtml:
A painless rib prominence with a scoliometer reading above about 7° in a girl who has not reached menarche (much growth remaining) is likely adolescent idiopathic scoliosis. A standing posteroanterior radiograph of the whole spine measures the Cobb angle and skeletal maturity, which together decide between observation, bracing and surgery. MRI is reserved for red flags.

Takeaway: suspected scoliosis: standing full-spine radiograph for the Cobb angle; MRI only for pain, neurologic signs or atypical curves.

whyNot.B: MRI is for red flags such as pain, a left thoracic curve, rapid progression or abnormal neurologic findings, none of which she has.
whyNot.C: Bracing depends on the Cobb angle and skeletal maturity, which cannot be judged without radiographs.
whyNot.D: A premenarchal girl has rapid growth ahead, when curves progress most; waiting years risks missing a curve that bracing could control.
whyNot.E: Surgery is considered for large curves, usually above about 45–50°, which must first be measured.

items.objective: Obtain a standing spine radiograph to measure the Cobb angle in suspected adolescent scoliosis.

cards.front: Which Salter–Harris type is commonest?
cards.back: Type II: through the physis with a metaphyseal fragment.

cards.front: Which Salter–Harris types enter the joint?
cards.back: Types III and IV.

cards.front: Most specific fracture patterns for infant abuse?
cards.back: Classic metaphyseal lesions and posterior rib fractures.

cards.front: Why do pulses persist in compartment syndrome?
cards.back: Compartment pressure collapses veins and capillaries long before it exceeds arterial pressure.

cards.front: Timing and triad of fat embolism syndrome?
cards.back: 24–72 h after long-bone fracture: hypoxemia, neurologic change, petechiae.

cards.front: Primary blast injury affects which organs?
cards.back: Gas-filled organs: middle ear, lungs, bowel.

cards.front: Stages of fracture healing?
cards.back: Hematoma and inflammation, soft callus, hard (woven bone) callus, remodeling to lamellar bone.

cards.front: Nerve at risk with a midshaft humerus fracture?
cards.back: Radial nerve (wrist drop).

cards.front: Muscles supplied by the axillary nerve?
cards.back: Deltoid and teres minor.

cards.front: Which nerve is most often injured in supracondylar fractures?
cards.back: Anterior interosseous branch of the median nerve (no OK sign).

cards.front: Rotator cuff muscle that initiates abduction?
cards.back: Supraspinatus (suprascapular nerve).

cards.front: Ligament torn in a dashboard knee injury?
cards.back: Posterior cruciate ligament.

cards.front: Root compressed by a posterolateral L4–L5 disc?
cards.back: L5: weak great-toe extension, numb dorsum of the foot.

cards.front: Position of the leg in posterior hip dislocation?
cards.back: Shortened, flexed, adducted and internally rotated; sciatic nerve at risk.

cards.front: Cauda equina vs conus medullaris?
cards.back: Cauda equina: LMN, asymmetric radicular signs, gradual. Conus: sudden, symmetric, early sphincter loss, mixed UMN and LMN.

cards.front: Best test for suspected hip fracture with normal x-rays?
cards.back: MRI.

cards.front: Time target for hip fracture surgery?
cards.back: Within 24–48 hours.

cards.front: Displaced femoral neck fracture in an older adult: fix or replace?
cards.back: Replace (hemiarthroplasty or total hip arthroplasty).

cards.front: Should osteoporosis treatment wait for DXA after a hip fracture?
cards.back: No; start it promptly.

cards.front: First antibiotic for an open fracture?
cards.back: A first-generation cephalosporin as soon as possible, plus tetanus prophylaxis.

cards.front: How to transport an amputated part?
cards.back: Wrap in saline-moist gauze, seal in a plastic bag, place on ice (not directly on ice).

cards.front: Medication class to deprescribe first in an older adult who falls?
cards.back: Sedative-hypnotics (benzodiazepines, Z-drugs).

cards.front: Positioning after transfemoral amputation to prevent contracture?
cards.back: Regular prone lying; no pillow under the residual limb.

cards.front: First step for a femur fracture in a non-ambulatory infant?
cards.back: Skeletal survey and report to child protective services.

cards.front: Reduction maneuver for radial head subluxation?
cards.back: Hyperpronation, or supination with flexion.

cards.front: Typical age and findings of Legg–Calvé–Perthes disease?
cards.back: 4–8-year-old boy; painless limp; flattened, dense femoral head.

cards.front: SCFE: atypical features that suggest an endocrine cause?
cards.back: Age under 10 or over 16, thin build, bilateral slips (hypothyroidism, GH, renal disease).

cards.front: Scoliosis red flags that need MRI?
cards.back: Pain, left thoracic curve, rapid progression, neurologic signs, early onset.

cards.front: Scoliosis curve range usually braced in a growing child?
cards.back: About 25–40° Cobb angle.

cards.front: First test for suspected scoliosis on forward bend?
cards.back: Standing PA full-spine radiograph (Cobb angle).

cards.front: When to image acute low back pain?
cards.back: Only with red flags, or persistent symptoms after about 6 weeks in a candidate for intervention.

cards.front: Next step for saddle anesthesia and urinary retention with back pain?
cards.back: Emergency MRI and surgical decompression.

cards.front: Ottawa ankle x-ray criteria?
cards.back: Cannot bear weight for four steps, or bone tenderness at the posterior edge or tip of either malleolus, navicular or fifth metatarsal base.

cards.front: Sprain vs strain?
cards.back: Sprain: ligament. Strain: muscle–tendon unit.

cards.front: Neurogenic claudication is relieved by what?
cards.back: Sitting or bending forward (lumbar flexion).

cards.front: Rotator cuff tear vs tendinopathy on exam?
cards.back: Tear: true weakness and drop-arm or lag signs. Tendinopathy: pain with preserved strength.

cards.front: How to prevent hospital-acquired ankle contracture?
cards.back: Keep the ankle at 90° with positioning or splints and do daily range of motion.
